So I'm about 60 hours in and I pretty much only know Lina. I like her a lot because of her relatively low cool down and mana cost compared to the damage she does. I also really like the fact that she does an insane amount of damage very quickly. She is very squishy though. Thanks ahead of time.

Lion is very similar to Lina - has a stun and a burst nuke ulti. He's a bit more nuanced - one additional active ability, a hex, and his mana drain spell. Good sustain.

Skywrath Mage has good burst damage, a lot of zoning potential, and is better at supporting a tankier carry in lane. He's been my newer favorite to Lina, but I think she has better lategame potential and scales better with limited farm.

Earthshaker is very fun but you need to kind of learn his limitations as a melee hero.

All good heroes for new players.

The heroes that @nonethewiser are great (especially Skywrath Mage!). With Earthshaker, you'll have to be more conservative with your mana since he is a strength hero with a limited mana pool and some costly (but very powerful) spells.

Keeper of the Light was one of the first heroes I played and I think great for newer players. He doesn't fit your criteria exactly, but he can do a lot of damage with his Illuminate (especially in the early game, just make sure you don't steal the creeps from your carry) and has a spell that replenishes mana so you'll never be short. He is quite squishy though, but I'd recommend giving him a try.

Some other heroes that I'd say are particularly burst-y include Centaur Warrunner, who is relatively simple to play due to his tankiness, Queen of Pain, though she's usually a mid hero who does best when snowballing and has a devastating AOE ultimate, and Ursa, who can make supports disappear in the blink of an eye with his right clicks but also depends on the slows/stuns of his teammates.
Leshrac is also worth a mention, I feel like their playstyles as cores are very similar, although you don't have to be as far back as Lina.
I would suggest playing Storm Spirit, Skywrath Mage, Lion, Timbersaw, or Leshrac. They are all pretty fun and do a good amount of burst damage.

Amazon rainforest was home to millions before European arrival, says study

I did not see a study citation and, in fact, this article seems to go out of its way to name the authors or give the title of the study in question. So I will admit to my bias beforehand: This "Journalist" is a piece of shit. Spoiler: I found the apparent study, the article is bullshit. The "study" is also not a study but a literature review.

Here is what I found, an article from July 23 on the same subject. This sent me on a ridiculously difficult search with every single article mentioning the names "Michael Heckenberger" or "Eduardo Góes Neves" giving no actual citations, or linking to dead web pages. One such dead web-page is this cached page.

The paper this "news" website appears to be referencing is this one

Heckenberger, Michael, and Eduardo Góes Neves. 2009. Amazonian Archaeology. Annual Review of Anthropology 38:251-266.

Immediate dead-end paywall.

You will note, the study pointing out a lack of available evidence for vegetation disturbance is from 2015, and I quote

Recent data generated from investigations of soils sampled from underneath standing terra firme forests in parts of the western Amazon indicate ephemeral ancient human occupation and little vegetation disturbance there.

Was this region relevant to the study? No idea. The "Journalists" didn't actually quote enough of the relevant 2009 study for me to find out. What I instead did was use google magic and found a public resource that links to the PDF. AFAIK this is now public resource, as there's no copyright or notice or anything in the PDF I've no way of knowing.

So what does the study say? Well! The study itself is actually a review, and not the result of some active work of anthropology. This means it is taking already given studies and commenting on them - it is not the result of archaeology. In other words, the news article is bullshit. It actually describes Amazonian cultures as part of "regional polities" (nothing Gaspar de Carvajal) and I quote:

These findings suggest remarkable sociocultural diversity, although it seems likely that no large bureaucratic state or integrated macroregional political entity or empire ever developed in the area.

In conclusion, without discussing this "review" in far greater depth and in turn analyzing its own sources, there's no way to determine if the reviewer is reporting what is true. What we can go on are current archaeological findings which are inconsistent with what this review stating. Another point is, while the review abstract claims this collapsed after European involvement, it does not actually elaborate within the review nor cements the point. It's taken as a given. Whether these polities existed, where they existed, or any large settlements that may have existed, we don't seem to have confirmed evidence even now. We also have nothing beyond the "given" assumption that they collapsed due to contact with Europeans.

Disclaimer: This is coming from someone who knows nothing about the subject. I did my best in the size and time constraints, and hope I kept this small. If I were to go whole-hog and educate myself on all relevant topics and cited material, this post would become a book. Do your own research if you are truly curious. Also, this journalist is a cock.

Edit: This "Journalist" is a freelance writer. Whenever you have a freelance writer writing an article, it's for clicks. They're never going to bother to fact check.
